items.prompt: A production account must copy recovery points to a security account so a compromised production administrator cannot delete the only backup. Which AWS Backup design should be evaluated?
constraints: The accounts are in the same organization.
The security account owns the recovery boundary.
The copy must use a separate vault policy.

options.text: Configure an AWS Backup cross-account copy to a vault owned by the security account, authorize the copy and destination vault, and test that the destination recovery point can be restored by the recovery role.
Keep the copy in the production vault and add a tag because tags make a recovery point independent of the account administrator.
Use a public S3 bucket because public visibility prevents the production account from deleting the backup.
Copy only the backup job logs because logs are sufficient to recreate the encrypted recovery point without source access.

feedback.Reason: A cross-account AWS Backup copy creates a recovery point in an independently governed destination vault.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The source backup plan or copy rule sends a recovery point to a destination account and vault. Destination access, encryption, retention, and restore permissions must all align.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security account limits deletion and administration, monitors copy status, and rehearses restore without depending on production administrators.
Details.errorCorrection: Tags do not change account ownership, public storage is unsafe, and job logs are evidence rather than backup data.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Cross-account copies improve blast-radius isolation but add copy cost, KMS and vault policy dependencies, and operational ownership work.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A tag does not move ownership or protect a recovery point from the production account boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Public storage increases exposure and is not an independent protected backup design.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Backup logs cannot recreate the encrypted recovery point without the backup data and keys.

items.prompt: A multi-account organization wants one account to manage backup policies and visibility centrally without granting that account unrestricted root-level access to every member account. Which capability should be used?
constraints: AWS Organizations governs the accounts.
The central account needs backup management and reporting.
Member-account boundaries must remain explicit.

options.text: Use AWS Backup delegated administration through AWS Organizations, then scope the delegated account’s operational permissions and retain member-account governance controls.
Share the management account root credentials because centralized backup requires root access to every member account.
Use one IAM group in the management account because IAM groups automatically administer resources in every member account.
Use a VPC peering connection because network reachability grants the central account backup administration.

feedback.Reason: AWS Backup delegated administration supports centralized organization-level management without treating root credentials as the operating model.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Organizations can designate a delegated administrator for supported AWS Backup management tasks. IAM and resource policies still govern actions and account boundaries.
Details.scenarioApplication: The organization registers the delegated account, scopes its roles, monitors member coverage, and keeps break-glass access separate from routine operations.
Details.errorCorrection: Root sharing is unsafe, IAM groups do not cross account boundaries automatically, and network connectivity does not confer backup permissions.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Delegation simplifies central governance but requires clear ownership, service support checks, and evidence of what the delegated account can actually manage.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Root credentials should not be shared or used as the routine central-management mechanism.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM groups are scoped to an account and do not automatically grant member-account access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: VPC peering provides network paths and does not grant AWS Backup API authorization.

items.prompt: A destination backup vault should accept copies only from two approved production accounts and should deny deletion by ordinary workload roles. Which control is closest to that boundary?
constraints: The vault is in a recovery account.
Copy sources are known by account or organization.
Workload roles must not administer the vault.

options.text: Use an AWS Backup vault access policy with explicit principals and actions for approved copy and recovery workflows, and separately protect vault administration and retention.
Use a security-group inbound rule because a vault access policy is only a network firewall rule.
Use an IAM policy in each source account and assume it automatically overrides the destination vault’s resource policy.
Make the vault public so all approved accounts can copy backups without policy maintenance.

feedback.Reason: An AWS Backup vault access policy is the resource-side control for constraining who can access a vault and which actions are allowed.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Vault policies work with identity policies and organization or account conditions to control cross-account copy and recovery access. They do not replace Vault Lock or key policies.
Details.scenarioApplication: The recovery account permits only approved backup-service roles and restore operators, tests denied deletion, and reviews the policy when accounts change.
Details.errorCorrection: Security groups are network controls, a source IAM Allow cannot bypass a destination explicit Deny, and public vault access violates the boundary.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A tight vault policy improves isolation but can block legitimate restore or copy operations if service principals, accounts, or actions are incomplete.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A vault access policy is a resource policy, not a security-group rule.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Cross-account authorization requires both sides to permit the action; a source Allow does not override a destination Deny.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Public access is incompatible with a restricted recovery boundary.

items.prompt: A backup plan copies recovery points from a workload account to a central vault and then to a second Region. What must the architect verify before calling the chain complete?
constraints: Each hop may have a different account or Region.
The final copy is the disaster-recovery boundary.
Every copy must remain decryptable and restorable.

options.text: Verify each copy rule’s source, destination vault, supported resource, encryption key, retention, permissions, completion status, and final restore procedure rather than assuming the first copy implies the second.
Verify only the first copy because AWS Backup automatically chains every recovery point to every configured Region and account.
Delete the source recovery point after the first copy because deletion confirms the destination has become authoritative.
Use DNS failover because a DNS record automatically creates and validates backup-copy chains.

feedback.Reason: A multi-hop copy design has independent service, policy, key, retention, and restore dependencies at each hop.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Backup copy jobs produce destination recovery points only when the configured source, destination, permissions, key, and resource support align. Copy success and restore success are separate evidence.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team monitors each hop, protects final copies, and restores from the last destination without depending on the source account.
Details.errorCorrection: Copy chains are not implied by one successful job, deleting the source is unsafe, and DNS controls traffic rather than creating recovery points.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More copies increase isolation and regional resilience but multiply cost, lag, policy surface, and restore-test requirements.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Each copy rule and destination must be configured and verified; a first copy does not imply a second.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deleting the source before testing the destination can destroy the only usable recovery point.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS failover changes endpoint routing and does not create or validate backup copies.

items.prompt: The recovery Region must preserve monthly copies for seven years while the source Region keeps daily copies for 30 days. How should the policy be expressed?
constraints: Source and destination have different retention duties.
Monthly copies must survive source cleanup.
Cost and compliance owners approve the policy.

options.text: Use separate backup rules or copy actions with explicit source and destination lifecycle settings so the destination monthly copies are retained independently of source daily expiration.
Set the source retention to seven years because destination retention cannot differ from source retention.
Delete destination copies after 30 days because any successful cross-Region copy is only a temporary transport artifact.
Use a route table tag to define seven-year retention because Regions infer backup policy from network tags.

feedback.Reason: Source and destination recovery policies can have different retention objectives and must be configured and evidenced separately.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Backup lifecycle applies to recovery points in the relevant vault or rule context; the destination copy must have retention that outlives source cleanup.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests that a daily source point expires without deleting the required monthly destination copy and records the ownership of each policy.
Details.errorCorrection: Source retention need not equal destination retention, a destination copy is not automatically temporary, and route tags do not govern backup lifecycle.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Long-term destination retention adds storage and compliance cost but provides an independent historical recovery boundary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Making source retention seven years is unnecessary and does not model the destination’s independent lifecycle correctly.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deleting destination copies after 30 days would violate the required long-term recovery policy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Network tags are not an AWS Backup lifecycle control.

items.prompt: A database team must give a recovery account access to an RDS manual snapshot, but the recovery account must ultimately own an independent copy. Which sequence is appropriate?
constraints: The snapshot is manual and encrypted or encryption requirements are known.
The source team must not own the final recovery copy.
The recovery account controls restore access.

options.text: Share the supported RDS snapshot with the recovery account, satisfy the snapshot and KMS permissions, copy it into the recovery account, and restore from the destination-owned copy.
Share the source database endpoint because an endpoint share transfers snapshot ownership without a copy.
Use an RDS read replica because a replica automatically becomes a destination-owned manual snapshot when the source account is compromised.
Make the snapshot public because public snapshots are the only RDS snapshots that can be copied cross-account.

feedback.Reason: Cross-account RDS snapshot recovery requires a supported sharing and copy flow, especially when the destination must own the final artifact.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Manual snapshots can be shared under RDS rules; encrypted snapshots require key permissions, and copying into the destination account establishes independent ownership.
Details.scenarioApplication: The recovery account copies and restores the snapshot, limits source access, and records the destination key and retention policy.
Details.errorCorrection: An endpoint is not a snapshot, a read replica is not the same as a retained snapshot copy, and public sharing is unsafe and unnecessary.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Copying creates a separate recovery artifact but adds storage, transfer, key, and restore validation work.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Sharing a database endpoint does not transfer snapshot data or ownership.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A read replica serves replication or read-scaling objectives and does not automatically become an independently owned historical snapshot.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Public sharing exposes data and is not required for controlled cross-account snapshot operations.

items.prompt: The source account must not be able to delete the final EBS recovery copy after a security handoff. What should the recovery account do?
constraints: The snapshot is shared or copied from another account.
The destination owns the incident recovery process.
Encryption permissions are controlled by the destination.

options.text: Copy the EBS snapshot into the recovery account and protect the destination-owned snapshot with the destination KMS key and IAM policy.
Leave the snapshot shared in the source account and rely on a source-account Deny that the destination cannot administer.
Copy only the EBS volume ID because the destination can recreate the blocks from the identifier.
Use a public AMI because AMI visibility transfers ownership of every source snapshot automatically.

feedback.Reason: Copying an EBS snapshot into the recovery account establishes a destination-owned recovery artifact and key path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The destination copy is managed by the destination account and can be encrypted with a destination key, reducing reliance on source-account lifecycle and permissions.
Details.scenarioApplication: Recovery operators test creating a volume from the copy and deny source-account principals any destination administration path.
Details.errorCorrection: A shared source snapshot remains subject to source ownership, an ID is not data, and AMI visibility does not automatically transfer snapshot ownership.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Destination ownership adds copy time and KMS policy coordination but materially improves account-boundary independence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A shared source snapshot remains owned and controlled in the source account.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: An EBS volume identifier does not contain the volume blocks needed for recovery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: AMI sharing and snapshot ownership are separate controls and public exposure is unsafe.

items.prompt: A central archive account must own all replicated S3 objects and prevent source-account ACLs from granting access in the archive. Which setting should be evaluated?
constraints: The destination bucket is in a separate account.
The archive account owns access decisions.
Object ownership must be consistent.

options.text: Use S3 Object Ownership with bucket-owner-enforced behavior where supported, configure replication ownership and bucket policies, and validate that the destination account controls the objects.
Keep ACLs enabled and grant the source account FullControl because source ownership is required for the destination account to read replicas.
Use a security group on the bucket because S3 object ownership follows the subnet that originated the request.
Use KMS key rotation as a substitute for object ownership because a rotated key transfers S3 object control.

feedback.Reason: S3 Object Ownership and replication settings can make destination ownership explicit and reduce ACL-based cross-account ambiguity.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Bucket-owner-enforced Object Ownership disables ACL-based ownership for the bucket and makes the destination account the owner of objects written there, subject to service and replication configuration.
Details.scenarioApplication: The archive account controls bucket policies, tests replicated object access, and removes source-account ACL assumptions from the design.
Details.errorCorrection: Granting broad ACL control preserves ambiguity, S3 buckets do not use security groups, and KMS key rotation does not transfer object ownership.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Ownership enforcement simplifies authorization but can require clients or replication configurations that still depend on ACL behavior to be updated.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Broad ACLs keep source-account ownership and access complexity instead of enforcing destination ownership.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 object ownership is not derived from VPC subnet or security-group membership.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: KMS key rotation changes cryptographic material handling and does not transfer S3 object ownership.

items.prompt: S3 objects must replicate from a workload account to a destination bucket owned by an archive account. Which authorization path should be reviewed?
constraints: The buckets are in different accounts.
The destination bucket policy is managed centrally.
The replication role must be least privilege.

options.text: Grant the S3 replication role only the required source read and replication actions, allow the destination bucket policy to accept that role, and test ownership and encryption together.
Grant every IAM principal in the source account s3:* because S3 replication uses the caller’s permissions for all future objects.
Grant only the destination account’s root user because a bucket policy cannot name a replication service role.
Use a route table association because cross-account replication is allowed when both buckets share a network route.

feedback.Reason: Cross-account S3 replication depends on a scoped replication role and compatible source and destination resource policies.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The replication configuration identifies a role that S3 assumes. Source permissions, destination bucket policy, ownership, and KMS permissions form one authorization chain.
Details.scenarioApplication: Security tests a new object, a filtered object, and a denied object while monitoring replication failures after policy changes.
Details.errorCorrection: Broad source permissions are unnecessary, the service role can be named in policies, and network routes do not authorize S3 bucket actions.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A narrowly scoped role reduces blast radius but requires maintenance when prefixes, keys, or destination policies change.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Replication should not grant s3:* to every source principal; S3 assumes the configured role.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The destination can authorize the replication role through its bucket policy; root-only access is not a sound operating model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 replication authorization is policy based and does not depend on shared network routes.

items.prompt: A DynamoDB table needs a retained recovery copy in another Region, but the application does not need active writes there. Which approach should be compared with Global Tables?
constraints: Historical recovery is the primary objective.
The destination need not serve current writes.
The copy must be restoreable and independently governed.

options.text: Use a DynamoDB backup or AWS Backup copy to the destination Region when supported, define destination retention and key ownership, and test restoring the table there.
Use Global Tables automatically because a live writable replica is always cheaper and simpler than a retained recovery copy.
Use DynamoDB Streams without a consumer because the service stores every stream record forever as a recovery table.
Use a VPC endpoint because a private endpoint copies DynamoDB data to every Region that can resolve its DNS name.

feedback.Reason: A retained backup copy is a closer match than an active multi-Region replica when the requirement is historical recovery rather than current write availability.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB backups or supported AWS Backup copy workflows create recovery artifacts with retention and restore semantics distinct from Global Tables replicas.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team compares RPO, restore time, destination capacity, key policy, and cost, then validates the destination restore process.
Details.errorCorrection: Global Tables add active replication and conflict design that may be unnecessary, Streams require consumers and are not indefinite backups, and endpoints do not copy data.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Backup copies are simpler for historical recovery but may have longer restore time than an active replica and do not provide continuous serving capacity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A live replica may be overkill and has different cost and consistency behavior than a retained backup copy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Streams are a change feed and are not an automatic indefinitely retained recovery table.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: VPC endpoints provide private network access and do not copy DynamoDB data between Regions.

items.prompt: The organization needs recovery points isolated from accidental or malicious deletion, with a defined delay before they become restorable. Which AWS Backup capability should be evaluated?
constraints: The service and Region support the capability.
The recovery account is separate from workloads.
The security team accepts additional restore workflow steps.

options.text: Evaluate an AWS Backup logically air-gapped vault, including its supported resources, copy workflow, retention, restore access, and delayed availability behavior.
Use a public vault because public visibility is the definition of logical air-gapping.
Use a security group with no inbound rules because network isolation alone creates a restorable backup vault.
Disable Vault Lock because logical isolation requires all recovery points to be immediately deletable by workload roles.

feedback.Reason: A logically air-gapped AWS Backup vault is designed for an additional isolation boundary and has specific supported-resource and restore behavior.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The vault separates recovery points from ordinary backup administration and can impose a delay or controlled process before recovery points are available for restore, depending on the feature configuration.
Details.scenarioApplication: Security verifies resource support, copy completion, retention, restore authorization, and the operational delay before relying on the vault during an incident.
Details.errorCorrection: Public access is the opposite of isolation, security groups do not create backup isolation, and deleting protection is not a requirement for air-gapping.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Logical air-gapping improves resilience against account compromise but adds supported-resource limits, storage cost, and recovery latency.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Public visibility exposes a vault and is not logical air-gapping.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Network isolation does not create or protect AWS Backup recovery points by itself.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Air-gapped recovery is intended to resist unauthorized deletion, not to make deletion easier for workload roles.

items.prompt: A cross-Region AWS Backup copy fails because the destination vault uses a customer managed KMS key. Which dependency is the likely design gap?
constraints: The destination vault is encrypted with a customer managed key.
The copy role is in the source account.
The destination security team controls key policy.

options.text: Review the destination KMS key policy, AWS Backup service permissions, source copy permissions, and any organization or vault policy conditions as one cross-account authorization path.
Rotate the key immediately because rotation grants the source copy role access to every new key version.
Remove encryption from the vault because encrypted backup copies cannot be transferred between Regions.
Add the source role to a security group because KMS key use is granted by VPC membership.

feedback.Reason: A destination customer managed key adds an explicit key-policy dependency to the backup copy authorization path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The backup service must be allowed to use the destination key for encryption and the relevant identities must be permitted by IAM, key, vault, and organization policies.
Details.scenarioApplication: Security grants only required key actions to the backup service or recovery roles, runs a test copy, and monitors key-policy changes.
Details.errorCorrection: Rotation changes key material and does not grant permissions, encryption can be used cross-Region when supported, and KMS is not authorized by security groups.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Customer managed keys improve control and audit evidence but create a failure dependency that must be included in copy and restore tests.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Key rotation does not change the principals authorized by the key policy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Encrypted backup copies can be supported; removing encryption would violate the stated protection requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: KMS uses IAM and key policies, not security-group membership, for key authorization.

items.prompt: A team selects a recovery Region solely because it is far from the primary Region. What else must the architect include in the decision?
constraints: The workload has data residency requirements.
The recovery Region must support the required services.
The recovery plan has an RTO and RPO.

options.text: Evaluate service and feature availability, data residency, latency and transfer paths, quota, capacity, key and backup support, cost, dependencies, and the tested recovery procedure.
Choose the farthest possible Region because geographic distance alone proves the best disaster-recovery design.
Choose the cheapest Region without checking whether the application services and backup features are available there.
Choose a Region that shares the same Availability Zones because cross-Region recovery requires identical AZ names.

feedback.Reason: Recovery-region selection is a system design decision that combines independence with compliance, capability, and operational feasibility.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A Region can be geographically independent but still fail the design through service gaps, residency violations, insufficient quota, key or backup limitations, or untested dependencies.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team records the decision matrix, reserves capacity where needed, configures copies and keys, and executes a regional restore exercise.
Details.errorCorrection: Distance alone is not enough, price cannot override capability or residency, and Availability Zone names are Region-specific.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A more suitable Region may cost more or have higher latency, but a cheap or distant Region that cannot restore the system is not a recovery solution.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Geographic distance is only one factor and does not prove service, compliance, or recovery feasibility.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A low price does not compensate for missing services, quotas, residency constraints, or untested recovery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Availability Zone identifiers are scoped to each Region and do not need to match across Regions.

items.prompt: During a regional incident, an operations role in the recovery account must restore a protected backup, but it must not delete vaults or change retention. Which permission shape is appropriate?
constraints: The role is used only during recovery.
The destination vault is protected.
Restore resources need their own service permissions.

options.text: Create a recovery role trusted only by the incident or operations identity, grant the minimum restore and destination-resource actions, and keep vault administration and deletion permissions separate.
Grant the role administrator access to every service because restore always requires unrestricted account permissions.
Grant only backup-list permissions because listing a recovery point automatically performs the restore in the target Region.
Use the source production role because cross-account recovery should preserve the source account’s identity boundary.

feedback.Reason: A recovery role should be scoped to restore workflows and trusted identities, while destructive vault administration remains separate.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Restore often requires AWS Backup and target-service permissions. Trust policy, identity policy, vault policy, key policy, and service-linked behavior must all align.
Details.scenarioApplication: Security rehearses the role in the recovery account, confirms the target resource permissions, and logs every restore action without granting deletion.
Details.errorCorrection: Unrestricted administrator access expands incident blast radius, list is not restore, and a source role should not be a hidden dependency for a destination-owned recovery process.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Least-privilege recovery roles require more design and testing but reduce the chance that an incident response action destroys protected backups.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Restore does not inherently require unrestricted account administrator access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Listing a recovery point does not restore it or authorize target-resource creation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A destination-owned recovery process should not depend on the compromised source role.

items.prompt: A security account will retain seven years of cross-account recovery copies. What should be part of the architecture review in addition to access policies?
constraints: The copies are independently owned.
Long retention creates storage and copy charges.
Finance requires charge visibility by workload.

options.text: Assign cost ownership for destination storage, copy and restore operations, use supported tags or account-level allocation, and monitor spend without weakening the recovery boundary.
Disable destination billing because security-owned backups are free when they are copied across accounts.
Put the recovery copies in the cheapest public bucket so the source account pays no storage cost.
Delete older copies whenever spend rises because cost alarms are a valid substitute for retention policy approval.

feedback.Reason: Independent recovery copies have real storage, copy, restore, and key costs that need explicit ownership and monitoring.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The destination account or vault typically incurs costs for retained recovery data and operations. Cost allocation and retention controls must be designed together.
Details.scenarioApplication: Finance maps backup spend to accounts or workloads, reviews lifecycle policy changes, and prevents budget alarms from silently deleting required recovery data.
Details.errorCorrection: Cross-account copies are not free, public buckets are unsafe, and cost alarms cannot replace approved retention governance.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Cost allocation adds tagging and reporting work but makes long retention sustainable and prevents security teams from becoming an unowned billing sink.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Backup storage and operations are billable according to service behavior; copying accounts does not make them free.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Public storage violates confidentiality and is not a sound cost-control strategy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Unapproved deletion can violate recovery and compliance requirements; cost controls must trigger review, not silent destruction.

items.prompt: The business requires a warm regional standby with low data loss, while also requiring a monthly immutable archive. Which combination best separates the objectives?
constraints: The standby must serve quickly.
The archive must resist logical deletion.
The two recovery objectives differ.

options.text: Use an appropriate service replication or multi-Region standby for the low-latency continuity objective and independently retained protected backups for the immutable historical archive.
Use only the immutable archive because an archive always provides the same RTO as a warm standby.
Use only active replication because a replica is always protected from application-level deletion and corruption.
Use a single DNS record because DNS TTL simultaneously defines RPO, RTO, retention, and immutability.

feedback.Reason: Warm continuity and immutable historical recovery are different objectives and usually require different controls.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Replication or standby reduces failover time and current data loss, while protected backups preserve historical points after logical errors or malicious deletion.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect sets separate RPO/RTO and retention requirements, tests both failover and restore, and documents which control is used for each incident type.
Details.errorCorrection: An archive may restore slowly, replication can propagate corruption, and DNS controls routing rather than data protection properties.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The combination costs more and adds operational complexity but avoids forcing one control to satisfy incompatible recovery goals.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An immutable archive does not necessarily provide the RTO of a warm standby.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Replication can propagate application-level corruption or deletion and is not a historical archive by itself.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS TTL affects name resolution and does not define RPO, retention, or immutability.

items.prompt: A destination recovery copy exists, but the organization has no evidence that it is complete, decryptable, or usable by the recovery account. What should close the gap?
constraints: The source is not required during the test.
The copy uses customer managed encryption.
Evidence must be repeatable.

options.text: Run an independent destination-side restore test, validate application data and key access, record copy and restore identifiers, and schedule recurring verification.
Check only the destination object count because counts prove encryption and application consistency.
Open the recovery copy publicly so an auditor can validate it without destination credentials.
Rotate the destination key and delete the old key immediately to prove the copy no longer depends on the source account.

feedback.Reason: A recovery copy is evidence-backed only when the destination can decrypt, restore, and validate it independently.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Restore testing exercises the destination vault, IAM, KMS key, resource service, data integrity, and application dependencies. Metadata counts are insufficient.
Details.scenarioApplication: The recovery account performs scheduled isolated restores, records test results, and alerts when a key, policy, or service change breaks recovery.
Details.errorCorrection: Counts do not prove integrity or decryptability, public access is unsafe, and deleting a prior key can destroy recovery.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Independent testing consumes resources but detects failures before an incident and provides audit evidence that copy completion alone cannot provide.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Object or recovery-point counts cannot prove key access, integrity, or application usability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Public access is not an acceptable audit mechanism for confidential recovery data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Key rotation and deletion must preserve decryptability; deleting the old key can make existing copies unusable.

items.prompt: A solution must recover from account compromise, regional outage, accidental deletion, and application corruption. How should the architect choose the copy pattern?
constraints: No single failure mode dominates the requirements.
Recovery time and recovery point objectives are documented.
Compliance requires independent retention.

options.text: Map each failure mode to controls: separate-account and cross-Region protected copies for isolation, replication or standby for continuity, point-in-time backups for logical recovery, and tested restore roles and keys.
Choose one cross-Region replica because geographic separation automatically covers account compromise, deletion, corruption, and retention.
Choose one immutable archive because immutability automatically supplies low-latency serving and zero data loss.
Choose public snapshots because broad access makes every recovery scenario easier to operate.

feedback.Reason: Recovery architecture is a mapping from failure modes to distinct protection and recovery mechanisms, not a search for one universal copy.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Account and Region separation reduce correlated control-plane risk, replication supports continuity, backups preserve history, and tested IAM/KMS paths make recovery executable.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architecture documents RPO/RTO, copy ownership, retention, restore runbooks, and the boundary that each control covers.
Details.errorCorrection: A replica can inherit corruption or account dependencies, an archive may be slow to restore, and public snapshots create a confidentiality incident.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Layered recovery costs more and requires more testing, but it avoids an unprotected failure mode hidden behind a single service choice.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A replica does not automatically provide independent retention or protection from logical errors and account compromise.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: An immutable archive does not promise low-latency serving or zero data loss.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Public snapshots increase exposure and do not make recovery safer.
